name: Wittelsbach
summary: Dukes of Bavaria since 1180 and Counts of the Rhine, the house gave emperors, electors, kings of Sweden and a network of branches that reach until the eighteenth century.
origin: Otto de Wittelsbach received the Duchy of Bavaria in 1180 after the fall of Henry the Lion. His grandson Otto II added the Palatinate of the Rhine by marriage. In 1329 the Treaty of Pavia separated the Bavarian line from the palatine, which would preserve the electoral dignity recognized by the Golden Bull of 1356.
history: Louis IV of Bavaria was king of Romans and emperor, faced with the papacy of Avignon; Rupert of the Palatinate was king of Romans between 1400 and 1410. Bavarian partitions (Landshut, Munich, Ingolstadt, Straubing) met with Albert IV in 1505. In the Thirty Years' War, Frederick V of the Palatinate lost Bohemia and his electorate, which passed to Maximilian I of Bavaria.
legacy: The branch of Zweibrücken gave the kings of Sweden Charles X Gustavo, Charles XI and Charles XII. Charles Albert of Bavaria was emperor as Charles VII (1742–1745) against Maria Theresa. In 1777 Charles Theodore, of the Palatinate, inherited Bavaria as well and reunited the two lines.

name: Jagelón
summary: Grand Dukes of Lithuania who by union with Poland in 1386 also reigned in Krakow and, at the end of the 15th century, in Bohemia and Hungary.
origin: Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, was baptized and married in 1386 to Eduviges, Queen of Poland, taking the name Ladislaus II. The personal union allowed him to defeat the Teutonic Order in Grunwald (1410) with his cousin Vitautas.
history: Ladislaus III was also king of Hungary and died in Varna (1444) against the Ottomans. Casimirus IV regained Western Prussia in 1466 and placed his sons on the thrones: Vladislaus in Bohemia (1471) and Hungary (1490), and John Albert, Alexander and Segismund I successively in Poland.
legacy: Louis II, son of Vladislaus, died in Mohács (1526) and his crowns passed to Ferdinand of Habsburg, married to his sister Anna. Sigismundo II Augusto signed the Union of Lublin (1569), which created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and died childless in 1572; since then the kings were elected.

name: Dreux
summary: A Capetian branch that became a Breton ducal house and from which emerged two rival paths towards the succession of Brittany.
origin: Robert I, son of Louis VI of France, received Dreux. His grandson Peter married Alix de Thouars, heiress of Brittany. Breton access came from that marriage, while Peter's male ancestry linked with the French royal house.
history: John I and John II consolidated the ducal continuity. Their marriages with Blanca de Champaña and Beatrice of England connected Brittany with Navarre and with the Plantagenets. Arthur II had children of two marriages. The offspring of his son Guy de Penthièvre and that of Juan de Montfort were confronted when John III died.
legacy: The dispute of 1341 opened a long war. The Montfort, branch of the Dreux, retained the duchy after Auray's victory in 1364. Juana de Penthièvre transmitted her heritage to the offspring of her marriage to Charles de Blois.

name: Gonzaga
summary: The Gonzaga built a prestigious court in Mantua and extended their dominions by marriage and imperial concession.
origin: The Corradi da Gonzaga family accumulated property and charges in the Mantuan territory. Luis Gonzaga brought down the Bonacolsi in 1328 and obtained the city’s government. Their descendants turned the town’s captainship into a dynastic power, elevated to marquees in 1433.
history: The Marquis combined military service with alliances between the Italian states. Isabel de Este made the court a top artistic center. Frederick II received the title of Duke of Mantua in 1530 and, by his marriage to Margarita Paleolologo, the family acceded to Montferrat.
legacy: The death of Vincent II in 1627 opened a succession war that ended up favoring the branch of Nevers. Other lines ruled Guastalla and small neighboring principalities. The marriages of the Gonzaga princesses linked Mantua with Austria, Poland and Württemberg. The loss of the Mantuan government in 1707 closed the sovereign stage of its main branch.

name: Ascania
summary: A family with branches in Brandenburg, the Saxon duchies and the principalities of Anhalt, divided between different lines and titles.
origin: Ascania is the general name of the Askanier. Its lines from Brandenburg, Saxony-Lauenburg, Saxony-Wittenberg and Anhalt come from the same medieval family. Anhalt’s branch is part of Henry I, son of Bernardo de Saxony and grandson of Alberto el Oso. Successive partitions gave rise to several principalities.
history: Catherine and Dorothea were daughters of Magnus I of Saxony-Lauenburg; Barbara came from Saxony-Wittenberg. In Anhalt, John George II and Leopold I belonged to Dessau; John Louis I, Frederick Augustus and Christian Augustus, to Zerbst-Dornburg. John George II's marriage to Henry Catherine of Orange-Nassau connected the branch of Dessau with the Netherlands.
legacy: Catherine II was born Princess of Anhalt-Zerbst and acceded to the Russian throne in 1762, after her marriage to Peter III and the coup that deposed him. In another branch, Leopold of Anhalt-Dessau reached the rank of Field Marshal in the service of Prussia and retained his principality. Both careers extended the influence of the family beyond their German domains.

name: Rurikida
summary: The descendants of Rurik ruled the Rus principalities for seven centuries; their Moscow branch gathered the Russian lands and became extinct with Feodor I in 1598.
origin: The tradition places Rúrik in Novgorod in the ninth century. His descendants ruled Kiev and, after the fragmentation of the Rus and the Mongol invasion, a network of principalities subjected to the Golden Horde. Alexander Nevsky, prince of Novgorod and Vladimir, defeated Swedes and Teutonics and negotiated with the Mongols.
history: Daniel, son of Nevski, received Moscow. Ivan I obtained from the Horde the right to collect taxes and Dmitri Donskói defeated the Tatars in Kulikovo (1380). Ivan III incorporated Novgorod, stopped paying tribute to the Horde (1480) and married Sophia Palaiologina.
legacy: Ivan IV crowned Tsar in 1547, conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and ruled with extreme violence. With the death of his son Fiodor I in 1598 he ended the dynasty in Moscow; they followed the Time of Troubles and, in 1613, the Romanovs.

name: Dampierre
summary: The Dampierres linked several French lordships with Flanders, where they had to negotiate between the king of France and the Flemish cities.
origin: The lineage took its name from Dampierre, in Champagne. A marriage to Matilde of Bourbon gave it the possession of that lordship. William of Dampierre’s union with Margaret of Constantinople opened his children’s rights over Flanders.
history: The rivalry between the sons of Margarita, born of their marriages with Avesnes and Dampierre, faced the successions of Hainaut and Flanders. legacy: The Flemish cities and Guy's successors had a conflictive relationship with the French monarchy. Family heritage reached Margaret III of Flanders, wife of Philip the Bold. His inheritance of 1384 was essential for the expansion of the Valois-Burgundy in the Netherlands.

name: Châtillon
summary: A house with several branches whose Breton connection is explained by the marriage of Charles of Blois to Joan of Penthièvre.
origin: The Châtillon were a French noble house with several branches, one of which inherited Blois County and was linked to the ducal succession of Brittany through Charles of Blois.
history: Charles de Blois defended the rights of his wife Joanna to the Duchy of Brittany. Her daughter Maria married Louis I of Anjou, creating a path between the Breton dispute and the Angevin expansion. Later, Françoise de Châtillon married Alain de Albret and was the mother of John III of Navarre and Carlota of Albret.
legacy: The Châtillon-Penthièvre links transmitted inheritances and succession rights to the Valois-Anjou and the Albret. Françoise's offspring became king in Navarre and retained interests on both sides of the Pyrenees.

legacy: The county passed through Mahaut’s heiresses to other houses and ended up integrated into the Burgundian lands. The descendants of the male branch followed their own trajectories as the county heritage was transmitted by female line.

name: Colleoni
summary: A family of the minor nobility of the Bergamo area that reached notoriety for the military career and patronage of Bartolomeo Colleoni.
origin: The family has been documented since the beginning of the 12th century in Bergamo. Its local possessions and networks provided Bartolomeo with a resource base and recruitment.
history: The family conquest of the castle of Trezzo in 1404 was a fleeting success in the face of the Visconti recovery. Bartolomeo then built his fortune as a condotiero, serving different Italian powers until he secured his position at the service of Venice. In 1454 he received command as captain general of the republic.
legacy: The religious and welfare foundations and the artistic patronage extended their memory. The Colleoni Chapel of Bergamo and the equestrian monument of Venice bear witness to this projection. The power of the house was supported by military lands and services, within the framework of broader states.
